People Who Never Reached Age 41

Franz Kafka

Birth date: July 2, 1883

Death date: June 2, 1924

Age: 40

Franz Kafka was a Prague-born German-language Jewish writer whose fiction transformed modern literature with visions of alienation, absurd bureaucracy, guilt, anxiety, and fragile identity. His best-known works include The Metamorphosis, The Trial, and The Castle, many of which became famous only after his friend Max Brod ignored Kafka’s request to destroy unpublished manuscripts. He died in 1924 at a sanatorium near Vienna after tuberculosis, especially affecting his throat, made eating extremely painful; he was 40 years old.

Edgar Allan Poe

Birth date: January 18, 1809

Death date: October 6, 1849

Age: 40

Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer, poet, editor, and critic whose tales of mystery and the macabre helped define Gothic fiction and the modern detective story. Best known for works such as "The Raven" and his short fiction, he became one of the most influential figures in early American literature. He died in Baltimore on October 7, 1849, aged 40, after being found in a distressed and confused condition; the exact cause of death remains unknown.

John Lennon

Birth date: October 8, 1940

Death date: December 7, 1980

Age: 40

John Lennon was an English musician, songwriter, artist and peace activist, best known as a founder, co-lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist of the Beatles and as one half of the Lennon–McCartney songwriting partnership. After the Beatles, he built a major solo career with songs such as "Imagine" and "Give Peace a Chance." He died in New York City on 8 December 1980 after being shot outside the Dakota apartment building, shortly after returning from a recording session.

Vincent van Gogh

Birth date: March 29, 1853

Death date: July 28, 1890

Age: 37

Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose bold colour, expressive brushwork and emotional intensity helped shape modern art. Although he worked seriously as an artist for only about a decade, he produced masterpieces including Sunflowers, The Starry Night and many self-portraits. He struggled with mental illness and poverty, and died in Auvers-sur-Oise after shooting himself, passing away two days later at the age of 37.

Death date: December 4, 1791

Age: 35

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian composer and musician of the Classical period, celebrated for operas, symphonies, concertos, chamber music, and sacred works that helped define Western music. A child prodigy from Salzburg, he later built his mature career in Vienna. He died there on 5 December 1791 at age 35 after a short illness; the exact medical cause remains uncertain, and his Requiem was left unfinished.

Martin Luther King Jr.

Birth date: January 14, 1929

Death date: April 3, 1968

Age: 39

Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister and civil rights leader whose advocacy of nonviolent resistance made him one of the defining figures of the U.S. civil rights movement. He helped lead the Montgomery bus boycott, co-founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, delivered the landmark “I Have a Dream” speech, and received the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize. In his final years, he broadened his work to address poverty and opposition to the Vietnam War. King was assassinated on April 4, 1968, in Memphis, Tennessee, while supporting striking sanitation workers and preparing the Poor People’s Campaign. He died at the age of 39.

Alexander Pushkin

Birth date: June 5, 1799

Death date: February 9, 1837

Age: 37

Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin was a Russian poet, playwright, and novelist, widely regarded as Russia’s greatest poet and a founder of modern Russian literature. His works, including Eugene Onegin, Boris Godunov, and Ruslan and Ludmila, shaped the literary language of 19th-century Russia. He died in Saint Petersburg at 37 after being fatally wounded in a duel with Georges d’Anthès, a French officer linked to rumors around Pushkin’s wife.

Che Guevara

Birth date: June 13, 1928

Death date: October 8, 1967

Age: 39
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Che Guevara is highly polarizing because he was a Marxist revolutionary and guerrilla leader associated with armed insurgency, political violence, revolutionary executions, and support for authoritarian communist rule in Cuba. Admirers view him as an anti-imperialist symbol, while critics emphasize repression, killings, and ideological extremism.

Ernesto “Che” Guevara was an Argentine Marxist revolutionary, physician, author, guerrilla leader, diplomat, and a central figure in the Cuban Revolution. He became one of the 20th century’s most recognizable political icons, associated with anti-imperialism, guerrilla warfare, and revolutionary internationalism. After leaving Cuba to promote revolutions abroad, he fought in Bolivia, where he was captured by Bolivian forces and executed on 9 October 1967 at the age of 39.

Birth date: May 31, 1926

Death date: August 3, 1962

Age: 36

Marilyn Monroe, born Norma Jeane Mortenson, was an American actress and model who became one of Hollywood’s defining icons of the 1950s. Famous for films such as Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, The Seven Year Itch, and Some Like It Hot, she combined comic timing, glamour, and vulnerability in a way that made her a lasting pop-culture figure. She died at age 36 at her Los Angeles home from a barbiturate overdose, and her death was ruled a probable suicide.

Alexander the Great

Birth date: July 19, 357 BCE

Death date: June 9, 324 BCE

Age: 32

Alexander the Great, king of Macedon and one of antiquity’s most influential commanders, inherited the throne at 20 and built an empire stretching from Greece through Egypt and Persia toward northwestern India. Undefeated in battle, he spread Greek political and cultural influence across much of the ancient world. He died in Babylon in June 323 BCE after a sudden illness, before securing a clear succession, leaving his empire to fragment among his generals. He was 32.

Frédéric Chopin was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the Romantic era, celebrated for transforming piano music through his nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises, études, preludes, and ballades. Born near Warsaw and later based in Paris, he became one of music’s earliest international celebrities while writing with a deeply personal, poetic style. Long troubled by poor health, he died in Paris on 17 October 1849 at the age of 39, most commonly attributed to tuberculosis, with later medical discussion suggesting complications involving tuberculous pericarditis.

In his final years he supported the Greek struggle for independence against the Ottoman Empire. He died in Missolonghi, Greece, after fever and illness, at the age of 36.

Blaise Pascal

Birth date: June 18, 1623

Death date: August 18, 1662

Age: 39

Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer whose work shaped projective geometry, probability theory, fluid mechanics, and religious philosophy. A prodigy from childhood, he designed early calculating machines and later wrote the influential Lettres provinciales and Pensées. After years of fragile health, his illness worsened sharply in 1662; he suffered convulsions in Paris, received last rites, and died the next morning at age 39.

Age: 37

Raphael, born Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino, was one of the defining artists of the High Renaissance, celebrated for the clarity, harmony, and grace of works such as The School of Athens, his Madonnas, and the Vatican Rooms. Alongside Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, he is remembered as part of the classic Renaissance triad. He died in Rome on April 6, 1520, at age 37, probably after a sudden fever or acute illness, while still at the height of his artistic powers.

Yuri Gagarin

Birth date: March 8, 1934

Death date: March 26, 1968

Age: 34

Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to travel into outer space. On 12 April 1961, aboard Vostok 1, he completed one orbit of Earth in a 108-minute flight, becoming an international symbol of the Space Race and a Hero of the Soviet Union. His only spaceflight made him one of the most celebrated figures of the 20th century. He died on 27 March 1968, aged 34, when the MiG-15UTI training aircraft he was flying with instructor Vladimir Seryogin crashed near Kirzhach; the exact cause remained disputed for decades.

Cleopatra

Birth date: January 12, 69 BCE

Death date: August 11, 30 BCE

Age: 39

Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and one of antiquity’s most politically skilled monarchs. A Greek-speaking queen from the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty, she ruled Egypt during the final crisis of the Roman Republic and allied herself first with Julius Caesar and later with Mark Antony. After Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra’s forces, Antony died by suicide, and Cleopatra followed shortly afterward in Alexandria, probably by poisoning, to avoid being displayed in a Roman triumph. She was 39 years old.

Death date: June 10, 1992

Age: 38

Rafael José Orozco Maestre was a Colombian vallenato singer and one of the defining popular voices of the genre. Born in Becerril, Cesar, he became famous as the lead singer and co-founder, with accordionist Israel Romero, of Binomio de Oro de América, a group beloved across Colombia, Mexico, and Venezuela. His warm, lyrical style made him a lasting icon of Colombian folk-pop music. He was shot dead outside his home in Barranquilla during his daughter’s quinceañera; later accounts linked the murder to jealousy and underworld connections, though some details remain disputed.

Swami Vivekananda, born Narendranath Datta, was an Indian Hindu monk, philosopher, author, and the leading disciple of Ramakrishna. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission and helped shape modern Hindu thought and Indian nationalism. After years of intense travel, teaching, and declining health, he died quietly at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, reportedly while meditating; a cerebral blood vessel rupture has been suggested as a possible cause.

Malcolm X, born Malcolm Little and later known as el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz, was an influential African American minister, public speaker, and Black nationalist leader. Arthur Rimbaud was a French poet whose fierce, visionary writing helped reshape modern poetry before he abandoned literature in his early twenties. Franz Peter Schubert was an Austrian composer who helped bridge the late Classical and early Romantic eras. Schubert died in Vienna on 19 November 1828 at the age of 31; the official diagnosis was typhoid fever, though later writers have discussed other possible causes.

Charlotte Brontë was an English novelist and poet, one of the celebrated Brontë siblings, and the author of Jane Eyre, published in 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell. Amelia Earhart was an American aviation pioneer, author, and one of the most admired figures in early flight. Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician and writer best known for her visionary work with Charles Babbage on the Analytical Engine. Her notes on the machine included what is often described as the first published computer program, and she also understood that such machines could manipulate symbols beyond numbers. Maximilien Robespierre

Birth date: May 5, 1758

Death date: July 27, 1794

Age: 36
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Maximilien Robespierre is highly controversial because he is closely associated with the Reign of Terror during the French Revolution, political repression, revolutionary tribunals, and mass executions by guillotine. His defenders point to his democratic, anti-slavery, and egalitarian positions, but his name remains strongly linked to state violence and ideological extremism.

Maximilien Robespierre was a French lawyer, Jacobin politician, and one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution. He championed political equality, universal male suffrage, civic virtue, and the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade, while becoming closely associated with the Committee of Public Safety and the Reign of Terror. In July 1794, amid rising fear of his power and policies, he was overthrown in the Thermidorian Reaction, arrested, and guillotined in Paris without trial at the age of 36.

Robert Burns

Birth date: January 24, 1759

Death date: July 20, 1796

Age: 37

Robert Burns was Scotland’s national poet, a brilliant lyricist in Scots and English whose works include "Auld Lang Syne", "Tam o’ Shanter", "To a Mouse", and "A Man’s a Man for A’ That". Born in Alloway to a farming family, he turned everyday rural life, love, satire, and radical sympathy for ordinary people into poetry with lasting international appeal. He spent his final years in Dumfries as an excise officer while continuing to collect and reshape Scottish songs. His health declined sharply in 1796; modern experts often link his death to endocarditis, probably connected with earlier rheumatic fever. He died in Dumfries on 21 July 1796, aged 37.

Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann was a German mathematician whose ideas transformed analysis, number theory, complex functions, and differential geometry. His work on Riemann surfaces, the Riemann integral, and the Riemann hypothesis helped shape modern mathematics and later influenced the geometry used in general relativity. He died of tuberculosis in Selasca, Italy, during a journey made for his fragile health, at the age of 39.

His relationship with Soviet cultural authorities became increasingly strained, especially after satirical works such as The Bedbug and The Bathhouse drew criticism. He died in Moscow on 14 April 1930 from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, leaving behind a career that remained politically celebrated yet personally turbulent.

Caravaggio, born Michelangelo Merisi, was an Italian painter whose intense realism, dramatic chiaroscuro, and tenebrism helped transform late Renaissance art into the Baroque style. Active mainly in Rome, Naples, Malta, and Sicily, he gave religious and mythological scenes a startling immediacy that influenced Rubens, Ribera, Velázquez, Rembrandt, and many others. His final years were turbulent after he killed Ranuccio Tomassoni and fled Rome. He died at 38 in Porto Ercole while trying to return toward Rome, traditionally reported as fever but still debated, with theories including infection, violence, or poisoning.

Joseph Smith Jr. was an American religious and political leader best known as the founder of Mormonism and the Latter Day Saint movement. He published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and organized a church that later developed into several denominations, including the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. His teachings, revelations, and leadership attracted many followers but also intense opposition. In 1844, after conflict in Nauvoo, Illinois, Smith was jailed in Carthage and was shot and killed by a mob at the age of 38.

Extremely controversial historical figure

His reputation is tied to political executions, alleged cruelty, persecution of Christians, violence within his own family, and the disputed but enduring association with the Great Fire of Rome. Some ancient accounts are hostile and partly propagandistic, but his public image remains strongly associated with tyranny and brutality.

Nero was the fifth Roman emperor and the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, reigning from AD 54 to 68. Remembered for his theatrical tastes, ambitious building projects, political violence, and the controversies surrounding the Great Fire of Rome, he remains one of antiquity’s most notorious rulers. Facing rebellion, abandonment by key supporters, and condemnation by the Senate, Nero fled Rome and died by suicide on 9 June AD 68 at the age of 30.

After a final illness in 1700, he named Philip of Anjou as heir and died in Madrid on 1700-11-01, aged 38, setting the stage for the War of the Spanish Succession.

Enver Pasha was an Ottoman Turkish military officer, revolutionary, and leading member of the Committee of Union and Progress. A central figure of the Young Turk movement, he became minister of war and one of the powerful Three Pashas who dominated the Ottoman Empire during World War I. In 9 CE he led a coalition of tribes that destroyed three Roman legions under Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, a defeat that helped halt Roman expansion east of the Rhine. In 21 CE, at about 37, he was assassinated by fellow Germanic nobles who feared his growing authority.

His life is known mostly from later writers such as Plutarch and Appian, and he became an enduring symbol of resistance against oppression. In 71 BC, his army was finally defeated by forces under Marcus Licinius Crassus; Spartacus is believed to have been killed in the final battle, though his body was never identified.

Guy Fawkes, also known as Guido Fawkes, was an English soldier and Catholic conspirator best remembered for his role in the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, a failed attempt to blow up the House of Lords and kill King James I. Born in York, he fought for Catholic Spain before joining Robert Catesby's conspiracy. After being discovered guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath Parliament, he was tortured, tried for high treason, and sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered. On 31 January 1606, he died at the gallows in Westminster, reportedly breaking his neck and avoiding the full brutality of the sentence.

After accepting a pardon and returning to piracy, he was cornered near Ocracoke by a force led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard. Caracalla, born Lucius Septimius Bassianus and later known as Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, was a Severan Roman emperor and the son of Septimius Severus and Julia Domna. His reign is remembered for the Antonine Constitution, which extended Roman citizenship to most free inhabitants of the empire, and for the monumental Baths of Caracalla in Rome. In 217, while campaigning in the East against Parthia, he was assassinated near Carrhae by a soldier, Justin Martialis, in a plot associated with the future emperor Macrinus.

Death date: April 30, 408

Age: 31

Arcadius was the Eastern Roman emperor from 383 to 408, first as co-emperor under his father Theodosius I and later as ruler of the eastern half of the empire while his brother Honorius ruled the West. His reign was marked less by personal command than by the influence of powerful ministers, court politics, Gothic pressure, and his wife Aelia Eudoxia. He died in Constantinople on 1 May 408, apparently from natural or unspecified causes, at about 31 years old, leaving the throne to his young son Theodosius II.

Birth date: June 20, 1962

Death date: August 14, 1990

Age: 28

Viktor Tsoi was a Soviet singer-songwriter, actor, and the iconic co-founder and frontman of Kino, the band that helped define late-Soviet rock. Born in Leningrad to a Russian mother and a Koryo-saram father, he became one of the most influential voices in Russian-language music; in August 1990, while in Latvia after a major concert period and working on new material, he died at 28 in a road collision when his car crossed into oncoming traffic.

Birth date: February 2, 1795

Death date: June 3, 1830

Age: 35

Antonio José de Sucre y Alcalá was a Venezuelan general and statesman, one of Simón Bolívar’s closest lieutenants and a leading commander in South America’s wars of independence. Celebrated as the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho, he helped secure independence for Ecuador and Peru and became Bolivia’s first constitutionally elected leader. After years of political tension in Gran Colombia, he was ambushed and shot dead near Berruecos on 4 June 1830, aged 35.

Li Wenliang

Death date: February 6, 2020

Age: 34

Li Wenliang was a Chinese ophthalmologist at Wuhan Central Hospital who became known worldwide after warning colleagues in late 2019 about early cases of a SARS-like illness that would later be identified as COVID-19. Reprimanded by local police for spreading alleged rumors, he continued treating patients, contracted the virus himself, and died in Wuhan on 7 February 2020 at the age of 34.

Death date: August 17, 1563

Age: 32

Étienne de La Boétie was a French Renaissance magistrate, humanist writer, poet, and political thinker whose Discourse on Voluntary Servitude became a striking early argument about tyranny, obedience, and the power people give to rulers. Closely linked to Michel de Montaigne, he died young in Germignan near Bordeaux after a severe illness, probably intestinal and sometimes described as plague-like, at the age of 32.

Michael Collins

Birth date: October 15, 1890

Death date: August 21, 1922

Age: 31

Michael Collins was an Irish revolutionary, soldier and politician who became one of the central figures in Ireland’s struggle for independence. He served as IRA Director of Intelligence, helped negotiate the Anglo-Irish Treaty, chaired the Provisional Government of the Irish Free State, and became commander-in-chief of the National Army. He died at age 31 during the Irish Civil War, when his convoy was ambushed by anti-Treaty forces at Béal na Bláth in County Cork.

Constantine IV

Birth date: December 31, 650

Death date: July 9, 685

Age: 35

Constantine IV was the Byzantine emperor from 668 to 685 and the eldest son of Constans II. His reign is remembered for checking Arab expansion, especially through the defense of Constantinople, and for convening the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which helped end the Monothelite controversy. In his final years he faced setbacks against the Bulgars and declining health; he died in Constantinople of dysentery in 685, at about 35, leaving the throne to his son Justinian II.

Birth date: January 14, 1795

Death date: February 10, 1829

Age: 34

Alexander Sergeyevich Griboyedov was a Russian diplomat, playwright, poet, composer, and linguist, remembered above all for the brilliant verse comedy Woe from Wit, one of the landmarks of Russian literature. As Russia’s representative in Qajar Persia after the Treaty of Turkmenchay, he became a symbol of both literary talent and imperial diplomacy. He died in Tehran when an angry mob stormed the Russian embassy, killing him and most of the mission staff amid anti-Russian anger and controversy over refugees sheltered at the legation.

Carole Lombard, born Jane Alice Peters, was an American actress celebrated for her sparkling comic timing and spirited roles in classic screwball comedies such as My Man Godfrey, Twentieth Century, Nothing Sacred, and To Be or Not to Be. Lombard died at 33 when TWA Flight 3 crashed into Mount Potosi, Nevada, as she was returning from a World War II war bond tour.

Nikolai Alekseyevich Ostrovsky was a Soviet-Ukrainian writer and committed communist whose novel How the Steel Was Tempered became one of the best-known works of socialist realism. Shaped by civil-war service, illness, and disability, he wrote despite paralysis and blindness. He died in Moscow on 22 December 1936, aged 32, after years of severe illness, leaving his second novel, Born of the Storm, unfinished.

Charles IV of France

Birth date: June 17, 1294

Death date: January 31, 1328

Age: 33

Charles IV of France, called Charles the Fair, was king of France and king of Navarre from 1322 to 1328 and the last ruler of the direct Capetian line. His reign saw conflict with Flanders, a failed bid for the imperial crown, and the War of Saint-Sardos against Edward II of England. He died at the Château de Vincennes at age 33, leaving no surviving son; his pregnant widow later gave birth to a daughter, and the succession passed to Philip VI of Valois, helping set the stage for later dynastic conflict.

Jovian

Birth date: December 31, 331

Death date: February 16, 364

Age: 33

Jovian, or Flavius Jovianus, was a Roman soldier who became emperor in June 363 after the death of Julian during the Persian campaign. His short reign is remembered for ending Julian’s anti-Christian direction and for concluding a costly peace with the Sasanian Empire, surrendering key eastern territories. While traveling toward Constantinople, Jovian died suddenly at Dadastana on 17 February 364, probably from suffocation or poisonous fumes in his sleeping quarters.

Liam Payne was an English singer and songwriter who rose to global fame as a member of One Direction, one of the most successful pop groups of the 2010s. Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor

Birth date: July 25, 1678

Death date: April 16, 1711

Age: 32

Joseph I was Holy Roman Emperor from 1705 to 1711 and a Habsburg ruler of Austria, Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia. The eldest son of Leopold I, he continued the War of the Spanish Succession and strengthened Habsburg influence in Italy through the victories of Prince Eugene of Savoy. He was also musically educated and is remembered as a reform-minded Baroque monarch. His reign ended abruptly during the smallpox epidemic of 1711; he became infected and died at the Hofburg Palace in Vienna at the age of 32.

Lawrence of Rome

Birth date: December 30, 225

Death date: August 9, 258

Age: 32

Saint Lawrence, also known as Lawrence of Rome, was one of the seven deacons serving the Christian community in 3rd-century Rome under Pope Sixtus II. Remembered for administering church goods and distributing aid to the poor, he became one of Rome’s most venerated early saints. During Emperor Valerian’s persecution of Christians in 258, Lawrence was arrested after Sixtus II and other clergy were killed; tradition says he was executed in Rome on a heated gridiron, a symbol that became central to his iconography.

Santa Faustina Kowalska

Birth date: August 24, 1905

Death date: October 4, 1938

Age: 33

Saint Maria Faustina Kowalska, born Helena Kowalska, was a Polish Catholic religious sister and mystic whose reported visions of Jesus inspired the modern Divine Mercy devotion, including the Divine Mercy image, chaplet, and feast. She lived mainly in convents in Warsaw, Płock, Vilnius, and Kraków, keeping a diary that became central to her spiritual legacy. In her final years she suffered from tuberculosis of the lungs and digestive system, spent time in a Kraków-Prądnik hospital, and died in Kraków-Łagiewniki on 5 October 1938 at the age of 33.

Death date: December 31, 1505 BCE

Age: 35

Amenhotep I was an early New Kingdom pharaoh of Egypt and the second ruler of the 18th Dynasty, remembered for consolidating power after the wars of liberation, campaigning in Nubia, rebuilding temples, and shaping royal funerary traditions. He ruled for about 21 years and was later worshipped as a patron deity at Deir el-Medina; modern CT analysis of his mummy suggests he died at about 35 years old, but no definite cause of death can be identified, and his body was rewrapped by priests after posthumous damage from tomb robbers.

Aaron Swartz was an American programmer, writer, and internet activist who helped shape RSS, the architecture of Creative Commons, web.py, Markdown, and Reddit, and later became a leading advocate for open access and digital rights through activism including Demand Progress; in 2013 he died by suicide in Brooklyn at age 26 while facing an aggressive federal prosecution over the mass download of JSTOR articles through MIT's network, a death that sparked lasting debate about prosecutorial pressure and internet freedom.

Gregory V

Birth date: December 31, 972

Death date: February 17, 999

Age: 27

Pope Gregory V, born Bruno of Carinthia, was the first German pope and ruled the Church from 996 to 999 during one of the most turbulent moments of the late 10th century. Chosen by his cousin, Emperor Otto III, he crowned Otto as Holy Roman Emperor, faced revolt in Rome, was driven out by enemies who backed the antipope John XVI, and returned after imperial intervention. He died suddenly in Rome in 999, probably of malaria though the exact cause remains uncertain, at about 27 years old.

Lucan

Lucan, born Marcus Annaeus Lucanus in Corduba in AD 39, was a brilliant Roman poet of Nero’s age and the author of the unfinished epic Pharsalia, a fierce retelling of the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey that made him one of the standout voices of Imperial Latin literature. After falling out with Nero and being implicated in the Pisonian conspiracy, he was forced to commit suicide in Rome in AD 65, reportedly reciting lines from his own poetry as he died.

André Marie Chénier was a French poet and political journalist whose refined, emotionally charged verse helped anticipate Romanticism while still drawing on classical models. Why this is controversial: Cesare Borgia is one of the most notorious figures of Renaissance politics. His legacy is associated with papal nepotism, military conquest, ruthless power-building, imprisonment, executions, suspected murders, and the amoral political image later linked with Machiavelli's The Prince.

Cesare Borgia was a Renaissance prince, former cardinal, condottiero, and one of the most notorious members of the Borgia family. The son of Pope Alexander VI and brother of Lucrezia Borgia, he tried to build a personal state in central Italy and became a political example for Machiavelli’s The Prince. After his father’s death, his power collapsed; he was imprisoned, escaped to Navarre, and was killed near Viana during a stormy military action, ambushed after outriding his own men.

Germanicus Julius Caesar was a celebrated Roman general and politician of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, admired for his campaigns in Germania, his popularity with the army and people, and his close place in the imperial family as the adopted son of Tiberius, father of Caligula, brother of Claudius, and grandfather of Nero. Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Egon Schiele is a substantially controversial figure because of his explicit erotic drawings, his use of very young models, and a 1912 criminal case in which he was jailed for offenses connected to public morality, while more serious accusations were dropped. His work remains artistically important but can raise concerns about sexuality, age, consent, and exploitation.

Egon Schiele was an Austrian Expressionist painter and draftsman, famous for jagged lines, psychological intensity, and provocative self-portraits and figure studies that helped define Viennese modernism. Mentored by Gustav Klimt, he produced many of his most important works in a very short career before dying in Vienna of Spanish flu on 31 October 1918, just three days after the death of his pregnant wife Edith; he was 28.

Jesse Woodson James was an American outlaw, former Confederate guerrilla, bank and train robber, and leader of the James–Younger Gang. Raised in Missouri’s divided borderlands, he became one of the most infamous figures of the post-Civil War West, later romanticized in popular culture despite the violence of his crimes. Murad IV was the Ottoman sultan from 1623 to 1640, remembered for restoring central authority with ruthless discipline, suppressing unrest in Istanbul, and leading the reconquest of Baghdad in 1638. Son of Ahmed I and Kösem Sultan, he first reigned under his mother's regency before taking full control. He died in Constantinople at 27 after a final illness, commonly reported as cirrhosis and in some accounts linked to gout.

Lee Harvey Oswald was an American former U.S. Marine whose life became inseparable from one of the most consequential events in modern history: the assassination of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas in 1963. Before that, he had defected to the Soviet Union, lived in Minsk, married Marina Prusakova, and later returned to the United States. Arrested after Kennedy's killing and the fatal shooting of Dallas police officer J. D. Tippit, Oswald denied responsibility and said he was a patsy. Two days later, while being transferred in police custody, he was shot and killed on live television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby.

Billy the Kid, born Henry McCarty and also known as William H. Bonney, was a young American outlaw and gunfighter of the Old West whose name became inseparable from New Mexico's Lincoln County War and the mythology of the frontier. After escaping jail while under sentence of death, he was tracked to Fort Sumner and shot by Sheriff Pat Garrett on July 14, 1881, dying at just 21 and becoming a legend almost immediately.

Birth date: October 8, 1907

Death date: February 22, 1930

Age: 22
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Horst Wessel is highly controversial because he was an SA activist and became a major Nazi propaganda martyr. His lyrics became the Nazi Party anthem, and his image was deliberately used by Joseph Goebbels and the Nazi movement to glorify political violence and National Socialism.

Horst Wessel was a German SA activist whose name became inseparable from early Nazi propaganda. Born in Bielefeld in 1907, he joined radical nationalist circles and rose within the Sturmabteilung in Berlin, where Joseph Goebbels later turned him into one of the movement's best-known martyr figures. Wessel is chiefly remembered because lyrics he wrote were turned into the 'Horst-Wessel-Lied,' which became the Nazi Party anthem. In January 1930 he was shot in the head in Berlin during a violent dispute involving Communist opponents and a conflict connected to his lodgings and unpaid rent; after weeks of treatment, he died from complications of the wound on 23 February 1930 at the age of 22.

Leo II was the child emperor of the Eastern Roman Empire in 474, grandson of Leo I and son of Zeno, raised to the throne to secure the dynasty during a tense political moment in Constantinople. After only a few months as emperor and co-ruler with his father, he died in the capital at about age 7 in late 474, most likely of natural causes, though later writers sometimes suspected poisoning because his death left Zeno as sole ruler.

Thomas Chatterton was an English poet, prodigy, and creator of the pseudo-medieval 'Rowley' poems whose brilliance and audacity made him a precursor of Romanticism and an influence on writers such as Keats, Shelley, Wordsworth, and Coleridge. Raised in Bristol in poverty, he published early, dazzled readers with forged medieval verse, and went to London seeking literary and political success. There, still only 17, he fell into desperate financial hardship and died by arsenic poisoning in 1770, a tragic end that helped turn him into one of literature's enduring doomed young geniuses.

Age: 19
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim is a highly contested figure because he led the Umayyad conquest of Sindh and Multan, an armed expansion that involved invasion, regime change, and the beginning of long-term Muslim rule in parts of the Indian subcontinent. He is praised in some traditions as a capable young commander and criticized in others as a conqueror whose campaign brought violence, subjugation, and enduring religious-political conflict.

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim was the young Umayyad general whose conquest of Sindh and Multan created the first lasting Muslim foothold in the Indian subcontinent. Appointed in his teens, he combined speed, siege warfare and political bargaining to defeat Raja Dahir and establish Umayyad rule, becoming one of the most consequential commanders of the early 8th century. His rise ended suddenly after a change of caliph: recalled in 715 during court rivalries tied to al-Hajjaj's faction, he was imprisoned and died soon afterward in Iraq, most commonly said to be at Mosul.

Lungtok Gyatso was the 9th Dalai Lama of Tibet, recognized in childhood and enthroned at the Potala Palace during a politically sensitive era when regents held much of the real power. His life was brief but symbolically important, and in 1815, after falling ill during the Monlam Prayer Festival—apparently from a severe cold that likely became pneumonia—he died in Lhasa at age 9.

Britannicus, born Tiberius Claudius Caesar Britannicus, was the son of the Roman emperor Claudius and Valeria Messalina, and for a time he stood near the center of the Julio-Claudian succession. Britannicus died in Rome at just 13, reportedly after being poisoned during a dinner shortly before his fourteenth birthday, in a death widely linked by ancient sources to Nero’s determination to remove a rival claimant.

Pavlik Morozov

Birth date: November 13, 1918

Death date: September 2, 1932

Age: 13
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Pavlik Morozov is highly controversial because Soviet authorities turned him into a Stalin-era propaganda symbol of loyalty to the state after he allegedly denounced his father during collectivization. Later historians have questioned major parts of the official story, and his legend remains associated with informing, family betrayal, state propaganda, and political martyr-making.

Pavel Trofimovich Morozov, known as Pavlik Morozov, was a Soviet peasant boy from Gerasimovka who became one of the most famous child figures of Stalin-era propaganda. He was celebrated across the USSR as a symbol of loyalty to the state after allegedly denouncing his father during collectivization; his story inspired books, songs, plays and monuments, even as later historians questioned parts of the official legend. In September 1932, at age 13, he was killed in his native village together with his younger brother, and his death was turned into a political martyr narrative.

Archduchess Maria Johanna Gabriela of Austria was a Habsburg archduchess, the eleventh child of Empress Maria Theresa and Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor. Did you know:

For most of history, a drink of water was also a gamble. Rivers, wells, and town pumps could carry sewage-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In the United States, typhoid fever was about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900; after water treatment, sanitation, and disinfection spread, it fell to 33.8 by 1920 and 0.1 by 2006. A glass of boring tap water may be one of the greatest inventions in history.

The humbling part is that this is not ancient history everywhere. WHO estimates that around 1 million people still die each year from diarrhoea linked to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hand hygiene. So when someone in a modern city turns a tap, showers, brushes teeth, and flushes a toilet without thinking, they are living inside a public-health miracle.
